name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SURFACECHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q01 - Ultra-clean metal surfaces and vacuum storage

questiontext.text: To obtain an ultra-clean surface of a metal for surface studies, a very high vacuum of the order of \(10^{-8}\) to \(10^{-9}\text{ Pa}\) is required. Why must such clean metal surfaces be stored in vacuum?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Clean metal surfaces possess unbalanced residual attractive forces and readily adsorb gas molecules from the surrounding atmosphere.

Step 2: Evaluation
If exposed to air, the major components of air—namely dioxygen (\(\mathrm{O}_2\)) and dinitrogen (\(\mathrm{N}_2\))—will immediately cover the clean metal surface.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Clean metal surfaces must be stored in vacuum to prevent them from being covered by dioxygen and dinitrogen molecules present in air.

answer.text: Otherwise they will be covered by molecules of dioxygen and dinitrogen from air.
Otherwise the metal surface will sublime rapidly at room temperature.
Otherwise the metal will dissolve completely into atmospheric moisture.
Otherwise the metal surface will convert into a homogeneous gas-gas interface.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SURFACECHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q02 - Absence of interface between two gases

questiontext.text: Why is there no interface between two bulk gaseous phases?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
An interface is a boundary separating two immiscible or distinct bulk phases.

Step 2: Evaluation
Gases are completely miscible with one another in all proportions, forming a single homogeneous mixture rather than two separate phases.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
There is no interface between gases due to their complete miscibility.

answer.text: Because gases have negligible molecular mass.
Due to complete miscibility between gases.
Because gas molecules cannot undergo adsorption.
Because gases exist only at very high vacuum.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SURFACECHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q03 - Definition of adsorbate, adsorbent, and desorption

questiontext.text: When \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) gas is taken in a closed vessel containing powdered charcoal, the pressure of the gas decreases. In this process, what are the correct terms for \(\mathrm{NH}_3\), charcoal, and the removal of adsorbed \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) from charcoal respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Adsorption is the accumulation of molecular species at the surface rather than in the bulk of a solid or liquid.

Step 2: Evaluation
The substance that concentrates at the surface (\(\mathrm{NH}_3\)) is the adsorbate, the material on whose surface adsorption occurs (charcoal) is the adsorbent, and the process of removing an adsorbed substance from the surface is desorption.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{NH}_3\) is the adsorbate, charcoal is the adsorbent, and removal of \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) is desorption.

answer.text: Adsorbent, adsorbate, sorption
Adsorbate, absorbent, absorption
Adsorbate, adsorbent, desorption
Desorbate, adsorbent, peptization

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SURFACECHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q04 - Distinction between adsorption, absorption, and sorption

questiontext.text: Which of the following correctly distinguishes absorption from adsorption?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Adsorption is a surface phenomenon, whereas absorption is a bulk phenomenon.

Step 2: Evaluation
In adsorption, the substance concentrates only at the surface (e.g., water vapour on silica gel), while in absorption, the substance is uniformly distributed throughout the bulk (e.g., water vapour in anhydrous calcium chloride). When both occur simultaneously, the process is termed sorption.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Water vapours are absorbed by anhydrous calcium chloride throughout its bulk, whereas they are adsorbed on the surface by silica gel.

answer.text: Water vapours are adsorbed by anhydrous \(\mathrm{CaCl}_2\) and absorbed by silica gel.
In absorption, the substance concentrates only at the surface without entering the bulk.
When a chalk stick is dipped in ink, the coloured dye penetrates uniformly to make the inside coloured.
Water vapours are absorbed by anhydrous \(\mathrm{CaCl}_2\) throughout its bulk, whereas they are adsorbed on the surface by silica gel.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SURFACECHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q05 - Origin of adsorption from unbalanced surface forces

questiontext.text: What is the fundamental cause of adsorption at the surface of a solid adsorbent?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Particles inside the bulk of an adsorbent are surrounded on all sides by similar atoms or molecules, so all forces acting on them are mutually balanced.

Step 2: Evaluation
In contrast, particles at the surface are not surrounded on all sides by atoms or molecules of their kind, so they possess unbalanced or residual attractive forces that attract adsorbate particles onto the surface.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Adsorption arises due to the unbalanced or residual attractive forces possessed by the surface particles of the adsorbent.

answer.text: Surface particles possess unbalanced or residual attractive forces because they are not surrounded by similar particles on all sides.
Bulk particles possess stronger residual attractive forces than surface particles.
Surface particles have higher entropy than the adsorbate gas molecules.
Adsorbate molecules diffuse rapidly into the crystal lattice to balance internal forces.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SURFACECHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q06 - Signs of enthalpy, entropy, and Gibbs energy in spontaneous adsorption

questiontext.text: For the spontaneous adsorption of a gas on a solid surface at constant temperature and pressure, what are the signs of \(\Delta H\), \(\Delta S\), and \(\Delta G\) respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
During adsorption, residual surface forces decrease and surface energy is released as heat, making the process exothermic (\(\Delta H < 0\)).

Step 2: Evaluation
When a gas is adsorbed, the freedom of movement of its molecules is restricted, so entropy decreases (\(\Delta S < 0\)). For the process to be spontaneous at constant temperature and pressure, \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\) must be negative (\(\Delta G < 0\)), which requires \(\Delta H\) to be sufficiently negative to overcome the positive \(-T\Delta S\) term.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\Delta H\) is negative, \(\Delta S\) is negative, and \(\Delta G\) is negative.

answer.text: \(\Delta H > 0\), \(\Delta S < 0\), \(\Delta G < 0\)
\(\Delta H < 0\), \(\Delta S < 0\), \(\Delta G < 0\)
\(\Delta H < 0\), \(\Delta S > 0\), \(\Delta G < 0\)
\(\Delta H < 0\), \(\Delta S < 0\), \(\Delta G > 0\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SURFACECHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q07 - Transition of physisorption to chemisorption with temperature

questiontext.text: How does the adsorption of dihydrogen on nickel change as the temperature is increased from a low value to a higher value?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A physical adsorption at low temperature may pass into chemisorption as the temperature is increased.

Step 2: Evaluation
Dihydrogen is first adsorbed on nickel at low temperature by weak van der Waals' forces (physisorption). As the temperature increases, molecules of hydrogen dissociate to form hydrogen atoms that are held on the nickel surface by chemical bonds (chemisorption).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Dihydrogen is first physisorbed on nickel at low temperature and then dissociates into hydrogen atoms held by chemisorption at higher temperature.

answer.text: It starts as chemisorption at low temperature and converts into physisorption at high temperature.
It remains purely physical adsorption at all temperatures without dissociation.
It is first adsorbed by van der Waals' forces (physisorption) and then dissociates to form hydrogen atoms held by chemisorption.
It is absorbed uniformly into the bulk of nickel without any surface interaction.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SURFACECHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q08 - Enthalpy and specificity of chemisorption vs physisorption

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding chemisorption?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Chemisorption involves chemical bond formation (covalent or ionic) between the adsorbate and the adsorbent.

Step 2: Evaluation
Chemisorption is highly specific, usually irreversible, has a high enthalpy of adsorption (\(80\text{--}240\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)), and increases with an increase in surface area. However, because it involves chemical bond formation, it results in a unimolecular layer, whereas physisorption forms multimolecular layers under high pressure.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The statement that chemisorption results in multimolecular layers under high pressure is incorrect.

answer.text: It is highly specific in nature and occurs only when chemical bonding is possible.
Its enthalpy of adsorption is high, in the range of \(80\text{--}240\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).
It increases with an increase in the surface area of the adsorbent.
It results into multimolecular layers on the adsorbent surface under high pressure.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SURFACECHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q09 - Critical temperature and extent of physisorption

questiontext.text: Which of the following gases is adsorbed to the maximum extent by \(1\text{ g}\) of activated charcoal at a given temperature and pressure?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In physical adsorption, easily liquefiable gases (those with higher critical temperatures) are readily adsorbed because van der Waals' forces are stronger near the critical temperature.

Step 2: Evaluation
Comparing the critical temperatures: \(\mathrm{SO}_2\) (\(630\text{ K}\)) > \(\mathrm{CH}_4\) (\(190\text{ K}\)) > \(\mathrm{H}_2\) (\(33\text{ K}\)). Therefore, \(1\text{ g}\) of activated charcoal adsorbs more \(\mathrm{SO}_2\) than \(\mathrm{CH}_4\), which is adsorbed more than \(\mathrm{H}_2\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{SO}_2\) is adsorbed to the maximum extent among the given gases.

answer.text: \(\mathrm{SO}_2\) (critical temperature \(= 630\text{ K}\))
\(\mathrm{CH}_4\) (critical temperature \(= 190\text{ K}\))
\(\mathrm{H}_2\) (critical temperature \(= 33\text{ K}\))
All three gases are adsorbed to the exact same extent because physisorption lacks specificity.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SURFACECHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q10 - Effect of pressure and temperature on physical adsorption

questiontext.text: Using Le-Chatelier's principle, which set of conditions favours physical adsorption of a gas on a solid?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Physical adsorption is a reversible exothermic equilibrium: \(\text{Solid} + \text{Gas} \rightleftharpoons \text{Gas/Solid} + \text{Heat}\).

Step 2: Evaluation
Increasing pressure reduces the volume of the gas and shifts the equilibrium forward, increasing adsorption. Since the process is exothermic, lowering the temperature shifts the equilibrium forward, whereas raising the temperature decreases physical adsorption.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
High pressure and low temperature favour physical adsorption.

answer.text: Low pressure and high temperature
High pressure and low temperature
High pressure and high temperature
Low pressure and low temperature

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SURFACECHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q11 - Activation energy in chemisorption

questiontext.text: Although chemisorption is an exothermic process, why is it very slow at low temperatures?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Chemisorption involves the formation of chemical bonds between the adsorbate and the adsorbent surface.

Step 2: Evaluation
Like most chemical changes, chemisorption requires a high energy of activation (which is why it is often called activated adsorption). At low temperatures, very few molecules possess sufficient energy to overcome this activation barrier, making the process very slow.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Chemisorption is very slow at low temperatures on account of its high energy of activation.

answer.text: Because van der Waals' forces vanish at low temperatures.
Because the surface area of the adsorbent decreases at low temperatures.
On account of the high energy of activation required for chemical bond formation.
Because \(\Delta S\) becomes positive at low temperatures.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SURFACECHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q12 - Probable range of 1/n in Freundlich isotherm

questiontext.text: In the Freundlich adsorption isotherm equation \(\frac{x}{m} = k \cdot p^{1/n}\), what is the probable range of values for \(\frac{1}{n}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Freundlich gave the empirical relationship \(\frac{x}{m} = k \cdot p^{1/n}\) with \(n > 1\).

Step 2: Evaluation
The factor \(\frac{1}{n}\) can take values between \(0\) and \(1\), with a probable range of \(0.1\) to \(0.5\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The probable range of \(\frac{1}{n}\) is \(0.1\) to \(0.5\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SURFACECHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q13 - Numerical calculation using Freundlich adsorption isotherm

questiontext.text: A plot of \(\log\left(\frac{x}{m}\right)\) against \(\log p\) for the adsorption of a gas on a solid gives a straight line with a slope of \(0.5\) and an intercept on the y-axis equal to \(\log_{10} 4\). What is the mass of gas adsorbed per gram of adsorbent \(\left(\frac{x}{m}\right)\) at a pressure of \(9\text{ atm}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Slope of the \(\log\left(\frac{x}{m}\right)\) vs \(\log p\) plot \(= 0.5\); y-intercept \(= \log_{10} 4\); pressure \(p = 9\text{ atm}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Model
The adsorption obeys the Freundlich adsorption isotherm over the given pressure range.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[\log\left(\frac{x}{m}\right) = \log k + \frac{1}{n}\log p \implies \frac{x}{m} = k \cdot p^{1/n}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
From the slope, \(\frac{1}{n} = 0.5 = \frac{1}{2}\).
From the y-intercept, \(\log_{10} k = \log_{10} 4 \implies k = 4\).
Substituting \(k = 4\), \(\frac{1}{n} = 0.5\), and \(p = 9\text{ atm}\): \[\frac{x}{m} = 4 \times 9^{0.5} = 4 \times \sqrt{9} = 4 \times 3 = 12\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The value \(\frac{x}{m} = 12\) is positive and consistent with \(\frac{1}{n} = 0.5\). Thus, the mass of gas adsorbed per gram of adsorbent is \(12\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SURFACECHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q14 - Limitation of Freundlich adsorption isotherm at high pressure

questiontext.text: Why does the Freundlich adsorption isotherm fail at very high pressures?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The Freundlich equation \(\frac{x}{m} = k \cdot p^{1/n}\) predicts that \(\frac{x}{m}\) continues to increase with pressure whenever \(\frac{1}{n} > 0\).

Step 2: Evaluation
Experimental adsorption isotherms always approach saturation at high pressure, meaning the adsorbent surface becomes completely covered and adsorption stops increasing with pressure. This saturation behaviour cannot be explained by the Freundlich isotherm.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The Freundlich isotherm fails at high pressure because it cannot explain the saturation of adsorption observed experimentally.

answer.text: Because \(\log\left(\frac{x}{m}\right)\) becomes negative at high pressure.
Because experimental isotherms approach saturation at high pressure, which cannot be explained by the Freundlich equation.
Because adsorption becomes endothermic at high pressure.
Because \(n\) becomes less than \(0\) at high pressure.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SURFACECHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q15 - Adsorption from solution phase

questiontext.text: When a precipitate of \(\mathrm{Mg(OH)}_2\) is formed in the presence of magneson reagent, it attains a blue colour. Which phenomenon is responsible for this observation, and how does the extent of adsorption from solution depend on temperature?

The blue colour of the \(\mathrm{Mg(OH)}_2\) precipitate is due to adsorption of the magnesium reagent on its surface. In adsorption from solution phase, the extent of adsorption decreases with an increase in temperature.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
It is due to adsorption of the reagent, and the extent of adsorption decreases with an increase in temperature.

answer.text: Absorption; extent increases with an increase in temperature.
Adsorption; extent increases with an increase in temperature.
Adsorption; extent decreases with an increase in temperature.
Peptization; extent is independent of temperature.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SURFACECHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q18 - Effectiveness of powdered adsorbents over crystalline forms

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Adsorption is a surface phenomenon, and the extent of adsorption increases with the increase of surface area per unit mass of the adsorbent at a given temperature and pressure.

Step 2: Evaluation
Powdered (finely divided) substances have a much larger surface area per unit mass compared to large crystalline solids, providing far more active surface sites for adsorption.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Powdered substances are more effective adsorbents because they have a much larger surface area per unit mass.

answer.text: Powdered substances have higher density than crystalline forms.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SURFACECHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q19 - Thermodynamic equilibrium temperature for adsorption

questiontext.text: During an adsorption process, at a certain stage the enthalpy of adsorption is \(\Delta H = -40\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\) and the entropy change is \(\Delta S = -100\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}\). At what temperature will this adsorption process attain equilibrium?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
\(\Delta H = -40\text{ kJ mol}^{-1} = -40000\text{ J mol}^{-1}\); \(\Delta S = -100\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
At adsorption equilibrium, the Gibbs energy change \(\Delta G\) becomes zero.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S = 0 \implies \Delta H = T\Delta S \implies T = \frac{\Delta H}{\Delta S}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[T = \frac{-40000\text{ J mol}^{-1}}{-100\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}} = 400\text{ K}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Units simplify cleanly to Kelvin (\(\text{K}\)), and \(400\text{ K}\) is physically reasonable. Thus, equilibrium is attained at \(400\text{ K}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Physisorption is reversible and decreases with increasing temperature, whereas chemisorption is irreversible and increases with increasing temperature.

answer.text: Both physisorption and chemisorption are reversible and decrease with increasing temperature.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SURFACECHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q23 - Identifying homogeneous catalysis

questiontext.text: Which of the following reactions is an example of homogeneous catalysis?

In homogeneous catalysis, the reactants, products, and catalyst are all in the same phase (liquid or gas).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SURFACECHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q26 - Rate acceleration during ester hydrolysis

Both electrophoresis and electroosmosis are electrokinetic phenomena observed when an electric potential is applied to a colloidal system.

In electrophoresis, colloidal particles move under an electric field, whereas in electroosmosis, the dispersion medium moves when particle movement is prevented.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SURFACECHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q56 - Mutual coagulation of oppositely charged sols

questiontext.text: What happens when a hydrated ferric oxide sol is mixed with an arsenious sulphide sol in almost equal proportions?

generalfeedback.text:

Mixing two oppositely charged sols in almost equal proportions neutralises their charges and leads to partial or complete precipitation (mutual coagulation).

Step 2: Evaluation
Hydrated ferric oxide is a positively charged sol, whereas arsenious sulphide (\(\mathrm{As}_2\mathrm{S}_3\)) is a negatively charged sol. When mixed, their charges neutralise each other and both precipitate out.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Both sols neutralise their charges and undergo mutual coagulation to form precipitates.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SURFACECHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q57 - Hardy-Schulze rule for coagulation of a negative sol

questiontext.text: Which electrolyte will have the lowest coagulating value (highest flocculating power) for the precipitation of a negatively charged \(\mathrm{As}_2\mathrm{S}_3\) sol?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A negatively charged sol is coagulated by cations. According to the Hardy-Schulze rule, the greater the valence of the flocculating ion, the greater is its flocculating power and the smaller is its coagulating value.

Step 2: Evaluation
The cations provided by the electrolytes are \(\mathrm{Al}^{3+}\) (from \(\mathrm{AlCl}_3\)), \(\mathrm{Ba}^{2+}\) (from \(\mathrm{BaCl}_2\)), \(\mathrm{Na}^+\) (from \(\mathrm{NaCl}\)), and \(\mathrm{K}^+\) (from \(\mathrm{K}_4[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_6]\)). Since \(\mathrm{Al}^{3+}\) has the highest positive valence (\(+3\)), it has the highest flocculating power and therefore the lowest coagulating value.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{AlCl}_3\) has the lowest coagulating value for a negatively charged \(\mathrm{As}_2\mathrm{S}_3\) sol.

answer.text: \(\mathrm{AlCl}_3\)
\(\mathrm{BaCl}_2\)
\(\mathrm{NaCl}\)
\(\mathrm{K}_4[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_6]\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SURFACECHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q58 - Coagulation of lyophilic sols and protective colloids

questiontext.text: Why does the addition of alcohol or acetone followed by a small quantity of electrolyte cause coagulation of a hydrophilic sol?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Lyophilic (hydrophilic) sols owe their stability to two factors: the charge and the solvation (hydration) of the colloidal particles.

Step 2: Evaluation
When solvents such as alcohol or acetone are added to a hydrophilic sol, dehydration of the dispersed phase occurs, removing the protective solvent sheath. Under this condition, a small quantity of electrolyte neutralises the charge and brings about coagulation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Alcohol or acetone causes dehydration of the dispersed phase, allowing a small quantity of electrolyte to coagulate the sol.

answer.text: Alcohol or acetone converts the hydrophilic sol into a protective colloid.
Alcohol or acetone dehydrates the dispersed phase, so a small quantity of electrolyte can neutralise the charge and coagulate it.
Alcohol or acetone increases the zeta potential of the hydrophilic particles.
Alcohol or acetone increases the Brownian movement so that particles settle down.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SURFACECHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q59 - Properties, dilution, and breaking of emulsions

questiontext.text: Which statement about emulsions is incorrect?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Emulsions are liquid-liquid colloidal systems (\(\text{O/W}\) or \(\text{W/O}\)) stabilised by emulsifying agents.

Step 2: Evaluation
Emulsions can be diluted with any amount of the dispersion medium, whereas adding the dispersed liquid forms a separate layer. The droplets are often negatively charged, show Brownian movement and Tyndall effect, and can be precipitated by electrolytes. Emulsions can be broken into constituent liquids by heating, freezing, or centrifuging—not by adding an emulsifying agent (which stabilises them).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The statement that emulsions can be broken into constituent liquids by adding proteins, gums, or soaps is incorrect.

answer.text: Emulsions can be diluted with any amount of the dispersion medium.
The droplets in emulsions are often negatively charged and can be precipitated by electrolytes.
An \(\text{O/W}\) emulsion can be broken into its constituent liquids by adding proteins, gums, or soaps.
Emulsions exhibit Brownian movement and Tyndall effect, and can be broken by heating, freezing, or centrifuging.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SURFACECHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q60 - Styptic action of alum and delta formation

questiontext.text: How do alum and ferric chloride solution stop bleeding from a fresh cut, and why does a delta form where a river meets the sea?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Both blood and river water (containing clay) are colloidal solutions that can be coagulated by electrolytes.

Step 2: Evaluation
Blood is a colloidal solution of an albuminoid substance; alum and \(\mathrm{FeCl}_3\) furnish high-valence cations (\(\mathrm{Al}^{3+}\), \(\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}\)) that coagulate blood to form a clot. River water is a colloidal solution of clay; electrolytes present in sea water coagulate the clay, depositing it to form a delta.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Both phenomena are due to coagulation of colloidal solutions by electrolytes.

answer.text: Both occur due to peptization of precipitates.
Both occur due to dialysis of impurities.
Both occur due to emulsification by protective colloids.
Both occur due to coagulation of colloidal solutions by electrolytes.
